title: Rachel's Tears and the New Covenant
summary: The LORD promises to bring both Israel and Judah home with singing: the scattered northern tribes will plant vineyards again, the blind and lame will walk on a level road, and Rachel, weeping for her lost children, is told to stop crying because they will return. Then comes the chapter's summit: God will make a new covenant, writing his law on their hearts, so that all will know him, and he will forgive their sins and remember them no more. The chapter ends with God's oath that Israel will endure as long as the sun and stars, and a vision of Jerusalem rebuilt and wholly holy.
story:
Chapter 31 is the heart of what readers call the Book of Consolation (chapters 30 to 33), the one long stretch of comfort in a book mostly given to warning. It opens with God telling Jeremiah to write his words in a scroll (30:2), as if this hope were meant to outlast the prophet's generation. Chapter 30 promised healing for a wound Jeremiah had called incurable; this chapter describes the healed people. Much of its first half speaks to Ephraim, the northern tribes lost to Assyria in 722 BC, so the hope reaches back more than a century to include those long given up for dead.

The high point, the new covenant of verses 31 to 34, answers the problem the whole book has diagnosed. Israel's heart was stubborn and its sin engraved there, “written with an iron stylus, engraved with a diamond point on the tablets of their hearts” (17:1), and the covenant Josiah had solemnly renewed in 622 BC (2 Kings 23:1-3) had not changed the people who swore to it. A merely restored nation would fail again. God's answer is not a better law but a changed heart, and a forgiveness so complete that God himself will not bring the old sins to mind. The next chapter turns the promise into an act, as Jeremiah buys a field in occupied Anathoth (32:6-15), and the promise itself becomes one of the central texts of the New Testament.
historical:
The chapter carries no date, and scholars place its parts at different moments. The poems addressed to Ephraim and Samaria (verses 2 to 22) fit Jeremiah's early ministry under Josiah (640 to 609 BC). Assyria was collapsing, and Josiah pushed north into the old territory of Israel, tearing down the altar at Bethel and the shrines in the towns of Samaria (2 Kings 23:15-20). A prophet in those years could speak of Ephraim's return as a real prospect. William Holladay (Hermeneia, 1989) argued that an early form of these chapters was addressed to the north in the later years of Josiah and was reworked for Judah after 587 BC. Others, including Robert Carroll (Old Testament Library, 1986), regard much of the Book of Consolation as the work of later editors in the exile. The present form clearly speaks to both houses (verses 27 and 31) and presupposes the fall of Jerusalem, so the collection was completed around or after the siege of 588 to 586 BC.

The north's disaster lay well in the past. Samaria fell in 722 BC after a three-year siege (2 Kings 17:5-6), and Sargon II's own inscriptions claim that he deported 27,290 people (27,280 in another copy) and resettled the land with foreigners. By Jeremiah's day the northern tribes had been scattered for a century, and many in Judah assumed they were gone for good. Judah's own collapse came in stages: the first deportation in 597 BC, which the Babylonian Chronicle dates to the second of Adar (March 16) of that year, and the destruction of the city and temple in 587 or 586 BC. Jeremiah 40:1 records that the Babylonians gathered the chained captives at Ramah before marching them north, and that Jeremiah himself was released there. Ramah, usually identified with the village of er-Ram about 8 kilometers (5 miles) north of Jerusalem, sat in Benjamin's territory on the main road north, so the town where Rachel is heard weeping was a real place of departure for exiles.

Rachel, the mother of Joseph and Benjamin, was the ancestress of Ephraim (Joseph's son) and of Benjamin. The Bible remembers her tomb in two ways. Genesis 35:19 says she was buried on the way to Ephrath, which a note identifies with Bethlehem, and the tomb on the Bethlehem road was already a pilgrim site when the Bordeaux Pilgrim passed it in AD 333. 1 Samuel 10:2 places her tomb at Zelzah in the territory of Benjamin, which would put it near Ramah. Either way Jeremiah's image works: the mother of the northern tribes and of Benjamin weeps from her grave as her descendants are led past.

Verses 38 to 40 trace the rebuilt city's limits by landmarks Jeremiah's hearers knew. The Tower of Hananel stood at the northeast corner, near the Sheep Gate (Nehemiah 3:1; 12:39), and the Corner Gate at the northwest (2 Kings 14:13; 2 Chronicles 26:9), so the line runs across the vulnerable north side. The hill of Gareb and Goah can no longer be located. The valley of the dead bodies and ashes is almost certainly the Hinnom Valley south of the city, where children had been burned in sacrifice and which Jeremiah called the Valley of Slaughter (7:31-32). The Kidron Valley runs along the east side, and the Horse Gate stood near the palace on the east (Nehemiah 3:28; 2 Kings 11:16). Zechariah 14:10 names the Tower of Hananel and the Corner Gate again as the limits of the restored city.
cultural:
The joy of verses 4 to 14 is the joy of a farming people at festival time. Virgin Israel takes up her tambourines (tuppim, small hand drums) and goes out dancing, as Miriam did after the sea (Exodus 15:20), as Jephthah's daughter did (Judges 11:34), and as the women did to greet David (1 Samuel 18:6). Women led such celebrations. The farmers of verse 5 will plant vineyards and ‘put them to common use’ (chillelu), a technical term: under Leviticus 19:23-25 a new vineyard's fruit could not be eaten for three years, was holy to the LORD in the fourth, and could be enjoyed from the fifth, and Deuteronomy 20:6 lets a man go home from war if he has planted a vineyard and not yet begun to use it. Jeremiah is promising years of peace, long enough to plant and wait and harvest. Deuteronomy's curses had included planting a vineyard and never enjoying it (Deuteronomy 28:30); here the curse is lifted on the very hills where it fell. The grain, new wine, and oil of verse 12 are the three staple crops that appear together throughout Deuteronomy as the gifts of the land.

The watchmen of verse 6 (notsrim) were lookouts posted on hilltops to warn of attack or to signal the new moon and festival days. Here they call northerners to go up to Zion, which is striking, since the north had worshiped at its own shrines at Bethel and Dan ever since Jeroboam set up golden calves there to keep his people from going to Jerusalem (1 Kings 12:26-30). Going up (the verb alah) was the ordinary word for pilgrimage, because Jerusalem lies high in the hills. The divided people will worship together again.

The family language runs deep. Ephraim was not Joseph's firstborn son, but Jacob crossed his hands and gave him the greater blessing (Genesis 48:14-20), and 1 Chronicles 5:1 says the birthright passed to Joseph's sons. God had called all Israel his firstborn son at the exodus (Exodus 4:22). In verse 11 God acts as ransomer (padah, to buy free) and redeemer (ga'al), the word for the kinsman who bought back a relative sold into debt slavery or a family field (Leviticus 25:25, 47-49); in the next chapter Jeremiah does exactly that for his cousin's land. Mourning, too, had its forms. Communities hired skilled mourning women (Jeremiah 9:17-20), and grief was voiced aloud and at length, so Rachel's refusal of comfort is the voice of a recognized lament. Striking the thigh (verse 19) was a gesture of grief, shame, or alarm (Ezekiel 21:12). The untrained calf that fights the yoke (verse 18) is a farming image Hosea had already used of Ephraim (Hosea 4:16; 10:11).

The proverb of verse 29, also quoted and rejected in Ezekiel 18:2, voiced the exile generation's complaint that they were paying for their ancestors' sins, drawing on the old formula of Exodus 20:5 and 34:7 about iniquity visited on the children. The picture is the sharp, puckering taste of unripe grapes. Deuteronomy 24:16 had already ruled that in human courts each person dies for his own sin, and Jeremiah promises that God's dealings will be felt the same way.

Covenants in the ancient Near East were formal, sworn relationships, often between a great king and a lesser one, written on tablets, deposited in a sanctuary, and read aloud at intervals. A copy of Esarhaddon's succession treaty of 672 BC, found in 2009 in a temple at Tell Tayinat in southeastern Turkey, shows such a tablet kept in a holy place. Israel's covenant followed the same shape: the tablets lay in the ark (Deuteronomy 10:1-5), and the law was to be read to all the people every seventh year (Deuteronomy 31:10-13). Deuteronomy itself had wanted these words ‘on your heart’ (Deuteronomy 6:6) and had promised that God would one day circumcise his people's hearts (Deuteronomy 30:6). Jeremiah's promise is that what was written on stone and kept in a box will be written inside each person. Teaching was the work of parents, priests, and prophets (Deuteronomy 6:7; Malachi 2:7), so a people who no longer need to urge one another to know the LORD would be a people whose whole religious order had been made new.
literary:
The chapter falls into two halves. Verses 1 to 22 are poetry, a chain of short oracles with shifting speakers; verses 23 to 40 are mostly prose, a series of promises three of which open with the formula “The days are coming” (verses 27, 31, and 38). The poems move from God's address to Virgin Israel (verses 2 to 6), to a call to sing among the nations (7 to 9), to a proclamation to the distant coastlands (10 to 14), and then to a scene with four voices (15 to 22): Rachel weeping, God answering her, Ephraim's confession quoted by God, and God's own yearning, closed by a call to Virgin Israel to come home. Phyllis Trible (God and the Rhetoric of Sexuality, 1978) read verses 15 to 22 as a single poem framed by female images, Rachel at the start and the woman who surrounds a man at the end, with Ephraim the son and God the parent at its center. The small word ‘again’ (od) runs through the whole chapter: again you will be built, again you will take up tambourines, again you will plant (verses 4 and 5), they will again speak this blessing (23), and the city will never again be uprooted (40).

The poems close on one of the hardest lines in the book: “a woman will shelter a man” (verse 22), literally ‘a female will surround a man’. It is introduced as something God has created (bara, the verb of Genesis 1, used only of God), and it is called a new thing (chadashah), the same word that will describe the covenant nine verses later. Its meaning is disputed, and the note on the text and the history below give the options. Verse 26, “At this I awoke and looked around”, suggests that at least some of what precedes came to Jeremiah in a dream or vision, a rare glimpse of how he received it; some interpreters take the voice to be the prophet's own, others read it as a remark by a later editor.

The prose promises are tied back to the book's opening. Verse 28 takes up the verbs of Jeremiah's call, to uproot and tear down, to destroy and overthrow, to build and plant (1:10), and the verb watch (shaqad) from the vision of the almond branch (shaqed), where God said he was watching over his word to perform it (1:11-12). God watched to tear down, and he will watch just as carefully to build. The new covenant passage (verses 31 to 34) is built as an announcement, a contrast (not like the covenant at the exodus), a positive statement of content, and a result, with two ‘no longer’ clauses and a closing ground clause introduced by ‘for’. It gathers the covenant formula that runs through the Law and the Prophets (Exodus 6:7; Leviticus 26:12; Jeremiah 7:23; 11:4; 24:7; 30:22). Verses 35 to 37 are two impossibility oaths: only if the fixed order of sun, moon, and sea failed, or the heavens could be measured and the earth's foundations searched out, would God reject Israel. The hymnic description of the Creator who stirs up the sea so that its waves roar also appears, in almost the same words, in Isaiah 51:15. The last promise (38 to 40) walks the boundary of the future city and ends by declaring holy the very valley that had been the place of the dead, with a last echo of the call verbs: it will never again be uprooted or demolished.

outline.t: The great homecoming and the joy of Zion
Rachel weeping, and hope for her children
Building and planting; no more sour grapes
Israel as lasting as creation; the city made holy

doctrines.note: The new covenant keeps the goal of the old, “I will be their God, and they will be My people” (verse 33), but changes the means: God will write his law within, give every member personal knowledge of himself, and forgive sin fully. It is new not because God's law changes but because God changes the people, and because the covenant rests from the start on his forgiveness rather than on their faithfulness.

“I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (verse 33) is the Old Testament's clearest promise of an inward renewal worked by God. With Ezekiel 36:26-27, where God gives a new heart and puts his Spirit within, it stands behind the New Testament's language of new birth and of the Spirit writing on hearts of flesh (2 Corinthians 3:3-6).

Ephraim's prayer, “Restore me, that I may return” (verse 18), shows repentance as both a human turning and a gift that must be asked for; the same verb, shuv, carries both. God's response is not reluctant pardon but a parent's yearning (verse 20), and the chapter's summit grounds everything in the promise to forgive iniquity and remember sin no more (verse 34).

The chapter insists that God has not finished with the scattered tribes or with Judah. He is Israel's Father and Ephraim is his firstborn (verse 9), and verses 35 to 37 bind his commitment to Israel's descendants to the fixed order of creation. Every Christian account of the new covenant has to reckon with this oath, as Paul does in Romans 9 to 11.

The chapter does not abolish God's law; it relocates it. “I will put My law in their minds and inscribe it on their hearts” (verse 33) takes the torah once carved on stone and kept in the ark and writes it within, fulfilling Deuteronomy's hope that God's words would be on his people's hearts (Deuteronomy 6:6; 30:6). The law becomes the shape of a renewed desire rather than a standard pressed on from outside.

words.note: Berit, covenant, a binding relationship with sworn commitments. It occurs about 287 times in the Old Testament and names God's covenants with Noah, Abraham, Israel at Sinai, and David, as well as treaties and marriages between people. The standard lexicons (BDB, HALOT) note that a berit is usually established by oath and often by a ritual. It appears five times in verses 31 to 33. Verse 31 is the only place in the Old Testament that uses the exact phrase new covenant (berit chadashah), though Jeremiah 32:40 and Ezekiel 37:26 speak of an everlasting covenant and a covenant of peace.

Chadash, new, fresh. The adjective occurs about fifty times, for a new house, a new song, a new king, new grain, and in Isaiah for the new things God is about to do (Isaiah 42:9; 43:19). The related noun chodesh names the new moon and the month, the moon that is the same moon renewed, which is why some scholars prefer ‘renewed covenant’. The text holds both ideas: this covenant is “not like” the one their fathers broke (verse 32), yet its content is the same torah, now written within. The same word marks the ‘new thing’ God creates in verse 22.

Torah, instruction, law. It occurs about 220 times and ranges from a parent's or teacher's instruction (Proverbs 1:8) to a priest's ruling to the whole body of Mosaic teaching. BDB and HALOT both begin from the sense of direction or teaching. Jeremiah does not promise a different torah but ‘My torah’ placed inside. The Septuagint translated it with the plural ‘laws’, which Hebrews 8:10 follows, and Christian interpreters have long debated how much of the Mosaic law this includes, a question the verse itself does not settle.

Yada, to know. One of the commonest verbs in the Hebrew Bible (about 940 times), it covers intellectual knowledge, skill, recognition, and the intimate knowledge of persons, including sexual union (Genesis 4:1). In covenant settings it means acknowledging and being loyal to someone; Jeremiah 22:15-16 defines knowing God as doing justice for the poor. In verse 34 it appears twice: no more urging ‘Know the LORD’, because all will know him. The promise is not that teaching will cease but that knowledge of God will no longer belong to a few.

Salach, to forgive, pardon. It occurs about forty-six times in the Old Testament, and in every case God is the one who forgives; people pardon one another with other words. It appears often in the laws of sacrifice (Leviticus 4:20, 26, 31) and in Solomon's prayer (1 Kings 8:30-50). In verse 34 it is the ground of the whole new covenant, introduced by ‘for’: God will forgive, and he will not remember their sin, which means not forgetfulness but a decision not to act on it.

Racham, to have compassion, used about forty-seven times, mostly of God. It is related to rechem, womb, and the plural rachamim, compassion, which is why many interpreters speak of a mother's feeling. In verse 20 it is doubled for emphasis, ‘I will surely have compassion on him’, and paired with the stirring of God's inward parts (me'ay, literally his bowels, the seat of deep emotion). Hosea 11:8 uses similar language of God's heart turning over for Ephraim. The word is especially fitting in a poem that begins with a mother weeping for her children.

Chesed, loyal love, steadfast love, covenant faithfulness; the BSB renders it “loving devotion” in verse 3. It occurs about 250 times and describes love that keeps its commitments and goes beyond them, the love God proclaims as his own name in Exodus 34:6-7. Paired here with ‘everlasting love’ (ahavat olam), it explains why God draws his people back: not because they have earned it but because his love has no end.

Ba'al, to be lord over, to marry, to be a husband. The verb occurs about fifteen times, and the noun ba'al means owner, husband, or lord, and was the name of the Canaanite storm god Israel so often worshiped. In verse 32 God says “I was a husband to them”, drawing on the marriage picture of Jeremiah 2 and 3, where Israel is a bride who became unfaithful. There may be a pointed play: Israel ran after the Baals, but the LORD was her true ba'al. The Septuagint read the line differently, as noted under the text.

christ:
This chapter stands behind some of the most important words of the New Testament. At the Last Supper Jesus took the cup and said, “This cup is the new covenant in My blood, which is poured out for you” (Luke 22:20; compare 1 Corinthians 11:25), and in Matthew's account he adds that his blood is “poured out for many for the forgiveness of sins” (Matthew 26:28), the very ground of Jeremiah's promise in verse 34. He was claiming that his death inaugurates what Jeremiah foresaw: a covenant resting on God's forgiveness, sealed not with the blood of animals as at Sinai (Exodus 24:8) but with his own. Paul calls himself a minister “of a new covenant, not of the letter but of the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:6), and in the same passage he contrasts tablets of stone with tablets of human hearts (2 Corinthians 3:3), drawing on this chapter and on Ezekiel 36.

Hebrews 8:8-12 quotes verses 31 to 34 in full, the longest continuous Old Testament quotation in the New Testament, to argue that Jesus is the mediator of a better covenant. It comments, “By speaking of a new covenant, He has made the first one obsolete” (Hebrews 8:13). Hebrews 10:15-18 returns to the closing promise and draws the conclusion that where sins have been forgiven, “an offering for sin is no longer needed” (Hebrews 10:18). Hebrews quotes the Greek translation, which in verse 32 reads differently from the Hebrew, a reminder that the New Testament writers usually used the Greek Bible of their day. Paul also hears the new covenant in Isaiah's promise that God will take away Israel's sins (Romans 11:27), which ties the chapter's promise to God's continuing purpose for Israel.

Matthew 2:17-18 quotes verse 15 after Herod's slaughter of the children of Bethlehem. Matthew's point is typological rather than predictive: the grief of Israel's mothers at the exile is heard again at the Messiah's birth, and in Jeremiah the lament is followed at once by the promise that the children will come home. Matthew places Rachel's voice at the start of Jesus' life because Jesus is the one in whom the exile ends and the new covenant begins. Other strands are thematic rather than quoted. The Father who yearns over a wayward son (verse 20) is the picture Jesus paints in the parable of the prodigal son (Luke 15:20). Jesus' saying that all will be taught by God (John 6:45) comes from Isaiah 54:13 but carries the same hope as verse 34. The chapter's larger direction, a people forgiven and knowing God from the least to the greatest, is what the New Testament says has begun in Christ and the Spirit and will be complete when he returns.
interpretation:
Jewish tradition has read this chapter above all through Rachel. Genesis Rabbah 82:10 explains that Jacob buried her on the road near Bethlehem, not in the family tomb at Hebron, because he foresaw that the exiles would pass that way and she would pray for them. Lamentations Rabbah (Proem 24) tells how Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, and Moses pleaded with God after the temple's fall and were not answered, until Rachel reminded God that she had not let jealousy shame her sister Leah; God was moved and promised, for her sake, to bring Israel home, quoting verses 15 to 17. The Targum of Jeremiah renders Ramah as ‘the height of the world’ and turns Rachel's weeping into the lament of the house of Israel. In the synagogue, the chapter's opening (31:1-19 in Hebrew numbering) is the prophetic reading for the second day of Rosh Hashanah, and verse 20 (19 in Hebrew) is one of the verses of remembrance in the New Year's additional service. Medieval commentators such as David Kimhi (Radak) read the new covenant as the Sinai covenant kept at last, not a new law, and polemicists such as the Karaite Isaac of Troki (Hizzuk Emunah, sixteenth century) argued that the promise remains unfulfilled. Alon Goshen-Gottstein (Studies in Christian-Jewish Relations, 2020) has surveyed this Jewish reception.

The Qumran community called itself those who entered the new covenant in the land of Damascus (Damascus Document, CD 6:19; 20:12). Among Christians, Justin Martyr (Dialogue with Trypho 11, about 160) used verses 31 and 32 to argue that Christ is the new and final law. Augustine's On the Spirit and the Letter (412) made the law written on the heart central to his account of grace: the Spirit writes within what the letter commanded from without. Jerome's commentary on Jeremiah took verse 22 of the virgin conception. Calvin, whose lectures on Jeremiah were published in 1563, rejected that reading and stressed that the new covenant renews the substance of the old. Reformed covenant theology built on the chapter's contrast of covenants, and many Lutheran churches read verses 31 to 34 on Reformation Day. Bernhard Duhm's commentary (1901) denied the new covenant passage to Jeremiah as late prose; most later commentators, including John Bright (Anchor Bible, 1965) and Jack Lundbom (Anchor Bible, 2004), have defended its roots in the prophet.

Rachel's lament had a rich afterlife through Matthew. The medieval Latin plays of the Holy Innocents, such as the Ordo Rachelis of Freising and the Fleury Playbook, gave Rachel a sung lament, and the communion chant ‘Vox in Rama’ was set as a motet by Jacobus Clemens non Papa (1549) and Giaches de Wert (1581). In the Revised Common Lectionary, verses 7 to 14 are read on the second Sunday after Christmas and verses 31 to 34 on the fifth Sunday in Lent in Year B.
text:
Readers who compare Bibles will meet three kinds of difference in this chapter.

The numbering differs. Printed Hebrew Bibles count the first verse of this chapter as 30:25, so through the rest of the chapter the Hebrew verse numbers run one lower than English ones: Rachel weeps in 31:14 of a Hebrew Bible, and the new covenant is 31:30-33 rather than 31:31-34. Jewish writers therefore often cite the new covenant as Jeremiah 31:30-33. In the Septuagint, the ancient Greek translation, the whole chapter is chapter 38, because the Greek edition places the oracles against the nations after 25:13 rather than at the end of the book.

The Greek text is often different. The Septuagint of Jeremiah is about an eighth shorter than the Hebrew, and Hebrew fragments from Qumran (4QJer b and 4QJer d) show that it was translated from a genuine shorter Hebrew edition rather than simply abridged. In this chapter it reads the consonants of verse 8 so that the blind and lame (pisseach) become a feast of Passover (pesach); it replaces the riddle of verse 22 with ‘the Lord has created salvation for a new planting; in salvation people will go about’; it puts verse 37 before verses 35 and 36; and in verse 32, where the Hebrew says ‘I was a husband to them’ (ba'alti), it reads ‘and I disregarded them’, perhaps from a similar Hebrew verb, ga'alti, ‘I loathed’. Hebrews 8:9 quotes the Greek, so readers of Hebrews meet “and I disregarded them”, while readers of Jeremiah meet “I was a husband to them.” In verse 33 the Greek has ‘laws’ in the plural and ‘mind’ for ‘inner part’, and Hebrews follows it.

English renderings of verse 22 vary widely. The King James Version has ‘A woman shall compass a man’, the BSB “a woman will shelter a man”, the NIV ‘a woman will return to the man’, and the NRSV ‘a woman encompasses a man’. The Hebrew is not in doubt; the differences reflect interpretation. In verses 38 and 40 the Masoretic margin supplies a missing word (‘are coming’) and corrects an unknown word to shedemot, ‘fields’.

teach.big: The God who tore down his people will build them again, and he will do it by giving them what they could never produce themselves: hearts that know him, and sins forgiven and remembered no more.

outline.t: God's love for his people is older than their failure and longer than their exile; because it is everlasting, he draws them back.
God gathers the weakest first, the blind, the lame, and women in labor, and turns mourning into joy on a road where no one stumbles.
God does not scold Rachel's grief; he answers it with a promise, and hope is given to the one who refuses to be comforted.
Repentance is asked for as a gift (‘restore me, that I may return’), and it meets a Father whose heart already yearns for the child.
Restored worship and restored work belong together: the holy mountain and the fields and flocks are blessed at once.
The God who watched over judgment watches just as closely over rebuilding, and no one will be able to blame the past for their own sin.
The new covenant does what the old could not: it writes God's law within, makes knowing God common to all, and rests entirely on forgiveness.
God's faithfulness is as fixed as the sun and stars, and even the valley of death will be made holy to the LORD.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first treats the new covenant as a new law opposed to the old, as if Sinai were bad and grace replaced it. Jeremiah says the problem was a broken covenant and stubborn hearts, and the promise is ‘My law’ written within; what is new is the heart and the forgiveness, not a different God or a different standard of holiness. The second turns verse 34 into a reason to dismiss teachers, preaching, or the church's instruction, since ‘no longer will each man teach his neighbor’. The churches of the New Testament had teachers (Ephesians 4:11; James 3:1); the point is that knowledge of God will no longer be limited to a class or a few, not that teaching becomes pointless.

A third misuse lifts verse 3 or verses 16 and 17 out of the chapter as a private promise that a person's lost child or broken family will certainly be restored in this life. The promise was spoken to a people in exile about a national return, and while it reveals God's heart for the grieving, it does not guarantee a particular outcome. Teachers should also avoid the opposite error of reading the chapter as though Israel were simply replaced: verses 35 to 37 make God's commitment to Israel's descendants as firm as creation, and whatever position one holds on the church and Israel, contempt for the Jewish people finds no support here. Finally, verse 22 cannot bear the weight of a proof for the virgin birth; that reading has an honorable history but rests on the Latin rather than the Hebrew.
teach.pastoral: Verse 15 will press on parents who have lost children, to death, estrangement, addiction, or prison, and on those whose grief is being hurried by others. Teach it slowly. God does not rebuke Rachel's refusal to be comforted; he speaks to her, names her tears as ‘work’ that will be rewarded, and gives her a future. Say plainly that mourning is not a lack of faith. Verses 18 to 20 speak to people who feel their past has disqualified them, and to those carrying shame from their youth (verse 19): God remembers Ephraim not to condemn him but with compassion. For the scrupulous, who cannot believe they are forgiven, verse 34 is the heart of the chapter: God chooses not to bring forgiven sin to mind. Be careful with the father language in verses 9 and 20 for listeners whose own fathers were absent or cruel. The chapter pictures a Father whose heart yearns over his son, which may be the reverse of what they knew, and it can be named as such.

hard.q: The new covenant is promised “with the house of Israel and with the house of Judah.” How can Christians claim it, and has it really come?
hard.a:
The strongest objection comes from Jewish readers, and it is textual. The promise is addressed to Israel and Judah, not to the nations; it speaks of the Sinai torah written on hearts, not of a law set aside; and it describes a world in which no one needs to be told to know the LORD and every member of the covenant knows him. Medieval Jewish commentators such as David Kimhi read it as the covenant of Sinai at last kept faithfully, and the Karaite polemicist Isaac of Troki (Hizzuk Emunah, sixteenth century) argued that the church cannot be its fulfillment, since Christians still teach one another, still sin, and are mostly not Israel. Modern historical critics add that Jeremiah meant a national renewal after the exile, not a covenant for a future Gentile church.

Christians agree that Jesus inaugurated the new covenant through his death, since he said so at the Last Supper and Hebrews quotes this passage to explain it, and that believers from every nation share its forgiveness and its gift of the Spirit. They answer the objection in different ways. Many in the Reformed and covenant traditions hold that the church, Jewish and Gentile believers together in Christ, is the renewed Israel to whom the promise belongs, with its full scope awaiting Christ's return. Dispensational interpreters distinguish the church's present share in the covenant's spiritual blessings from national promises to ethnic Israel, including restoration in the land, still to come; some earlier dispensationalists, notably Lewis Sperry Chafer, went so far as to propose two new covenants, one for Israel and one for the church, a view most later dispensationalists have dropped. Progressive covenantalists such as Peter Gentry and Stephen Wellum (Kingdom through Covenant, 2012) see Christ as the true Israel in whom the promise is fulfilled for all who belong to him. Many across these traditions read Paul's argument in Romans 9 to 11 as expecting a future turning of Israel to Christ (Romans 11:26-27). On the charge that the promise has not come, most Christian interpreters answer that it has begun but is not complete: the Spirit now writes on hearts, forgiveness is now full, and the day when all know God without remainder lies ahead. This is a second-order question on which faithful Christians disagree. All should grant that verses 35 to 37 bind God to Israel's descendants as firmly as to the sun and stars, and all should reject contempt for the Jewish people, whom Paul calls “loved on account of the patriarchs” (Romans 11:28).

hard.q: Matthew says Herod's massacre fulfilled Rachel's weeping. Isn't he taking a verse about the exile out of context?
hard.a:
The objection has two parts. First, verse 15 plainly describes the exile of Rachel's descendants in the sixth century BC, not the killing of infants at Bethlehem six centuries later, and it is not phrased as a prediction at all. Critics from the Enlightenment onward have used this and Matthew's other formula quotations as evidence that the evangelist ransacked the Old Testament for proof texts. Second, the massacre itself is recorded nowhere outside Matthew, not even by Josephus, who catalogs Herod's cruelties at length, and scholars such as Raymond Brown (The Birth of the Messiah, 1977) have judged the story more likely to be a theological narrative patterned on Pharaoh's slaughter of Hebrew boys than a historical report.

Responses begin from what Matthew means by fulfill. Most commentators, including those who defend the story's history, agree that Matthew is not claiming Jeremiah foresaw Bethlehem. He reads Israel's history as a pattern that finds its fullness in Jesus, as he does with Hosea 11:1 in the same chapter, and his choice of this verse is careful: Ramah was where the exiles were gathered, Rachel's tomb was remembered near Bethlehem, and Jeremiah's lament is followed immediately by the promise that the children will return. Matthew hears in the massacre the old grief of exile and implies that the answer to it has now been born. On the history, R. T. France (Novum Testamentum 21, 1979) argued that in a village the size of Bethlehem the victims would have numbered perhaps a dozen or two, too few for Josephus to notice amid Herod's many killings, and that the story fits what is known of Herod's last years. Whether the account is taken as history, as most evangelical and many Catholic scholars take it, or as theological narrative, the reading of Jeremiah it reflects is a recognizable Jewish way of reading Scripture, not a misunderstanding of it.

observe: List the groups God says he will gather in verses 7 to 9. Why might the text name these people in particular?
In verses 31 to 34, what four things does God say he will do? Which one is introduced with ‘for’, as the reason for the others?
Trace the voices in verses 15 to 22. Who speaks, who is spoken to, and how does each speech answer the one before it?
interpret: Verse 33 promises God's law written on the heart. How is that different from knowing the law well, and why could the Sinai covenant not produce it on its own?
Why does the chapter follow the promise of a new covenant (verses 31 to 34) directly with God's oath about the sun, moon, and stars (verses 35 to 37)?
Ephraim prays ‘Restore me, that I may return’ (verse 18). What does that request say about who makes repentance possible?
apply: Rachel refuses to be comforted, and God does not rebuke her; he gives her a promise. How should that shape the way you sit with someone in grief?
The new covenant ends with God remembering sins no more. Which old failures do you keep bringing to mind that God has chosen not to?
The proverb about sour grapes blamed the previous generation. Where are you tempted to explain your own choices by what others did before you?
